lines: Light a match on Earth, and the flame stretches up.
Hot air rises... and drags fresh air in behind it.
Nothing rises. The flame turns small, round, and blue...
and it lives or dies on one thing: the air drifting past it.
NASA has been setting fires in space for decades. On purpose.
But the answers are locked inside test tables and two-hundred-page reports.
And the biggest question of all... how fire behaves on a Moon base... has never actually been tested.
The Moon question is still open
So we asked: what if an eight-year-old could investigate it... like a detective?
It starts in Mission Freefall. Flip gravity off... and watch the flame change right in front of you.
Then you build NASA's real wind tunnel, piece by piece.
A crew of guides walks you through it. And PIX, our little evidence robot, has a hint whenever you're stuck.
Every chapter has one real job to do.
Switch on AI vision, and the computer traces the flame and measures it, in pixels.
No made-up numbers. And it tells you when a frame is too bright to trust.
Now, a detective game. Which outline really matches this NASA photo?
Get it right, and a clue lights up.
Start with test B20. Turn the airflow down.
The atlas finds the real experiment, test B16... but it hides what happened.
So you have to predict first.
Then NASA's own words appear, with the exact page they came from. That's how real science works.
A future habitat might use thirty-four percent oxygen, at about half of Earth's air pressure.
Your job: sort four real clues onto the Evidence Ladder.
A small flame in ordinary air? Close... but different.
Tiny burning droplets? They explain how fire works. Not how plastic burns.
And the top rung... stays empty. Nobody has run this test yet.
A gap isn't a promise of safety. It's the next experiment.
A gap is the next experiment
You can ask PIX anything, and every answer points back to NASA's evidence.
And at the end, you don't get a generic score.
You get a list of exactly what you did... and a certificate with your name on it.
But the real evidence goes much bigger.
In NASA's Saffire experiments, an empty cargo ship left the space station... and NASA lit fires inside it.
Twenty runs, and every single number is traced to its exact line in a NASA table.
Saffire Six got closest to Moon-base air. Close... but not there.
Close to Moon air, not there
For mentors and judges, every question climbs the same ladder.
Direct. Analogous. Mechanistic. Or a gap. Different kinds of fire are never mixed into one table.
And any card can answer: why am I here?
Each condition, matched or missed... then the rung... then the NASA page it came from.
Every step, traced to a page
Compare two experiments, and it warns you they are not replicas.
The Research Frontier spells out what we know, what we don't, and the test that would close the gap.
Seventy-six test records. Fifty-four NASA findings, each quote checked word for word.
And all of it is open. Download the data... and check our work.
Real NASA data. A real adventure. And honest answers about what we still don't know.
